window.near: In a launch window: close to the {{ideal}} km²/s² of the ideal (Hohmann) transfer between these two orbits.
window.far: Far from a launch window: the ideal (Hohmann) transfer between these orbits needs about {{ideal}} km²/s². Windows come round about every {{months}} months, when Earth and Mars line up.

assumptions.Moon: Timing modelled on Apollo 11: about {{coast}} days' coast after leaving Earth orbit, then about {{orbit}} day in lunar orbit before landing. The path is a two-body orbit around the Earth (Lambert's problem) from a parking orbit to where the ephemeris puts the Moon; the Moon's own pull and course corrections are left out. The lunar-orbit loops are drawn, not computed.
assumptions.Mars: The launch date is the one that needs the least launch energy for this landing date, searching {{min}} to {{max}} days of flight. The path is a two-body orbit around the Sun (Lambert's problem) between where the ephemeris puts Earth at launch and Mars at landing; the planets' own pulls near departure and arrival are left out.

sources.title: Sources and methods
sources.intro: Every number in SiteLine is worked out from published data by code in this project; none is typed in by hand. This page brings together how each check works, how we tested it, and every dataset with its licence and link.

methods.positions: Where the Sun and the Earth are, seen from the Moon: NASA JPL's DE440 ephemeris, read with NAIF's SPICE toolkit by our pipeline into a table the app interpolates.
methods.horizon: What the ground hides: from each spot, the horizon is traced in every direction across NASA's LRO LOLA south-pole terrain.
methods.sun: Sunlight: through the {{days}}-day stay we step through time and measure how much of the Sun's disc clears that horizon. The site fails if less than {{pct}}% of the disc is up at any moment, and the moment it drops is found to the minute.
methods.earth: Earth in view, for talking to the lander: the same test for the Earth, counting {{rule}}.
methods.slope: Slope: a lander needs ground flatter than {{deg}}° over 100 m. Inside 83°S the slope is measured on LOLA’s 10 m terrain of the south pole, reading only the few tiles around the site: a plane fitted to the heights within 50 m gives the landing slope, and Horn’s method on each 10 m cell within 1 km gives how much of that 2 km area is under 20°, as steep as astronauts can walk. Outside 83°S, or if those tiles do not arrive, the report says it needs finer terrain instead of guessing.
methods.zone: Artemis zone: the spot must lie south of {{lat}}° latitude.
methods.longTerm: Long-term sunlight, Earth view and permanent shadow: NASA's maps from LOLA terrain (Mazarico et al. 2011, PGDA product 69) at 60 m, averaged to 360 m by our pipeline, which also works out the distance to the nearest permanent shadow from them. Until the pipeline has published them, the Landfall concept demo's 2.4 km maps.
methods.planets: The Worlds list and signal delays: distances from the DE440 planet table. A signal's time is that distance divided by the speed of light.
methods.facts: World facts: NASA's planetary fact sheets and NAIF's gravitational parameters. Gravity and escape speed are worked out from them.

earthRule.margin2deg: its centre at least 2° above the horizon

sources.more: The same list is CREDITS.md in the project, and each panel names its own sources too.

sound.cues: A few short sounds go with what you see, never instead of it: a rising major third when a site passes, one soft note while it is not decided yet, and a single low note when it fails; air for each camera flight, longer and brighter the faster the camera moves; on the way back out to the solar system, air that falls away as the worlds recede, then the opening's chord an octave lower as the whole system comes into view; a very quiet tick for each click of the phone's dial; and a small chime when the copilot answers.
sound.control: Browsers allow no sound until you tap or press a key, so once everything has loaded the opening asks for one tap to enter, and plays its sound with it. The speaker button in the header, or the M key, turns every sound off or on at once, and the choice is remembered in this browser.
sound.opening: The opening has its own sound, made to follow the picture: a low hum that builds with the loading, a glint each time the light catches the turning emblem, then air as it rushes past, a quick glide as the shooting star streaks off, a soft chord as its gold ring opens into the Earth’s orbit, and a small ping as the lander reaches the Moon.

fine.heading: Sunlight on NASA's 30 m terrain, which sites are judged on, agrees with NASA's own long-term maps within a point:
fine.note: NASA's maps (PGDA product 69, 60 m) and our 30 m horizon are independent computations on two LOLA products. The 1.2 km grid and Bussey et al.'s Kaguya-based study both give more sunlight: too coarse to see the gentle rises within a few kilometres that shade a site when the Sun sits a degree or two up.

panel.heading: Mars

panel.sources: Heights: NASA MGS MOLA (<megdr>MEGDR</megdr>, made by the MOLA Science Team and archived by the PDS Geosciences Node at Washington University in St. Louis) through <jaanga>Jaanga’s height-map tiles</jaanga>, © 2015 Jaanga authors, <ccby>CC BY 4.0</ccby>, resampled to a coarser grid (about 21 km), so peaks and floors can read a few hundred metres off. Slope shading is computed from these heights, so it has no finer detail than they do.
